articles.title: Chunking YouTube transcripts for RAG, with timestamps that link back
articles.excerpt: If you're building search or Q&A over videos, the fiddly part isn't the embeddings - it's turning caption lines into chunks that still know where in the video they came from. This is a chunker for tha…
articles.body: If you're building search or Q&A over videos, the fiddly part isn't the embeddings - it's turning caption lines into chunks that still know where in the video they came from. This is a chunker for that. It's standard library Python, and every chunk keeps a timestamp and a deep link so an answer can cite "0:05" and open the video right there. Originally published at importly.io . Why not embed the caption lines directly Transcripts arrive as short segments. Caption tracks give you one segment per on-screen line, often five to ten words; speech-to-text gives roughly one per sentence. Embedding each one separately makes retrieval worse: a five-word line carries too little meaning to match a question, and you end up storing thousands of vectors per hour of video.

articles.title: A 10% review queue that catches 94.1% of failures: predictive maintenance on AI4I
articles.excerpt: Maintenance and reliability teams often face the challenge of deciding which assets to inspect first when resources are limited. In this project, I developed a predictive-maintenance analytics pipelin…
articles.body: Maintenance and reliability teams often face the challenge of deciding which assets to inspect first when resources are limited. In this project, I developed a predictive-maintenance analytics pipeline that turns sensor telemetry into a ranked work queue. The most concrete measured result is the review queue performance: reviewing the top 10% of assets (200 machines) captures 94.1% of all holdout failures . This represents a 9.4x lift over a random review strategy. You can find the full implementation in the smart-factory-app repository . Problem Maintenance teams cannot review every asset equally. The goal was to determine if sensor telemetry could create a ranked work queue capturing most failures within a limited budget, expressed in terms of cost.

articles.title: Claude Code Worktrees Filling Your Disk? How to Find and Remove Leftover Git Worktrees
articles.excerpt: Note: Originally published at getcleanbit.app. Written by the CleanBit developer with AI assistance. All measurements were taken on a real developer Mac. Claude Code and Codex worktrees fill up your M…
articles.body: Note: Originally published at getcleanbit.app . Written by the CleanBit developer with AI assistance. All measurements were taken on a real developer Mac. Claude Code and Codex worktrees fill up your Mac because Git shares commit history across worktrees, but never shares untracked build directories like node_modules , Rust target/ , Swift .build/ , or Python .venv/ . Every parallel agent task that runs npm install , cargo build , or swift build inside its own git worktree creates a fresh multi-gigabyte copy of dependencies—and those folders stay on disk even after your PR is merged unless you remove the worktree with git worktree remove or clear its build directories.

articles.title: Hide API keys behind a Cloudflare Worker
articles.excerpt: Every client that talks to an API ends up holding a key, and every copy of that key is another place it can leak. The pattern I use to avoid that: hide the key behind a Cloudflare Worker on the free t…
articles.body: Every client that talks to an API ends up holding a key, and every copy of that key is another place it can leak. The pattern I use to avoid that: hide the key behind a Cloudflare Worker on the free tier. The client calls the Worker. The Worker adds the real key server-side and forwards the request to the upstream API. The client never sees the key, and the Worker URL is the only credential it needs. The problem: keys multiply until one leaks It starts with one script and one key. Then the key is in an environment file, then in a config, then in a notebook, then in a chat log because someone needed to debug quickly. Each copy is a separate leak surface, and keys leak exactly once — after that, the damage is done.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 24, 1947: The US Navy launches the 1st Aerobee sounding rocket, but it didn't reach space
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 24, 1947, the U.S. Navy launched the first Aerobee rocket into the sky, but it never reached space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 24, 1947, the U.S. Navy launched the first Aerobee rocket into the sky, but it never reached space. Aerobee was a suborbital sounding rocket designed to study Earth's atmosphere . After World War 2, the United States started reusing erman V-2 rockets for this kind of research. When they started running out of V-2 rockets , the United States constructed its own rockets that were similar but cheaper to build and to launch. In the weeks leading up to the first Aerobee mission, three test flights were launched. Those tests used a dummy version of Aerobee with a live booster to see if the two stages would separate properly. On Aerobee's first real flight, the rocket flew about 35 miles high. That's below the 62-mile (100 kilometers) upper limit for the boundary of space .

articles.body: Explore This Section Science Citizen Science Amateur Astronomer? Be a… Overview Resources Opportunities Citizen Science Highlights About Science Activation Neutron stars are the ultra-dense, city-sized leftovers of dead stars. When they collide, they can release a brief flash of light called a kilonova . These immensely powerful events forge much of the universe’s gold, platinum and other heavy elements. Since a kilonova fades within days, astronomers have to find it fast, and no single observatory can watch the whole sky. But if you have a telescope with a camera, or access to one, you can help find and follow these cosmic fireworks as a part of NASA’s Kilonova Catcher project! Kilonova Catcher connects amateur astronomers around the world into a rapid-response network.

articles.title: NASA’s Northrop Grumman CRS-25 Mission Overview
articles.excerpt: NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25 mission, or Northrop Grumman CRS-25, will deliver about 11,000 pounds of science and supplies to the International Space Station. The mission wi…
articles.body: NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25 mission, or Northrop Grumman CRS-25, will deliver about 11,000 pounds of science and supplies to the International Space Station. The mission will be the third flight of the company’s Cygnus XL, the larger, more cargo-capable version of the company’s solar-powered spacecraft. The Cygnus XL will launch aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. Following arrival to the station, astronauts aboard the space station will use the Canadarm2 to grapple the spacecraft before ground controllers robotically install it to the Unity module’s Earth-facing port for cargo unloading.

articles.title: Raising the stakes for enterprise networks with AI modernization
articles.excerpt: Enterprise networks are under severe strain. As companies rush to deploy artificial intelligence, the technology is quickly becoming the biggest source of demand on the network. Now, agentic AI is add…
articles.body: Enterprise networks are under severe strain. As companies rush to deploy artificial intelligence, the technology is quickly becoming the biggest source of demand on the network . Now, agentic AI is adding to the load. Tasks conducted by AI agents generate an estimated 450% more network traffic than the same tasks done by human workers. As AI inference shifts from hyperscale training clouds—the huge centralized data centers where raw AI models ingest vast datasets and learn—to real-time, latency-sensitive applications, the need for on-premises or near-premises infrastructure grows. As a result, the gap between enterprise networks that are ready to support AI and those that are not is widening.
